title: They Meant It for Evil, But God Meant It for Good
paragraphs:
They Meant It for Evil, But God Meant It for Good
The Hidden Depth of Genesis 50:20 That Changes How You See Betrayal, Suffering, and Your Entire Story
Some wounds never fully leave you.

The betrayal.
The humiliation.
The rejection you never deserved.
The people who smiled while secretly pushing you toward the pit.
Years pass. Life moves forward. You learn how to function. You learn how to smile again. Yet there are moments when old memories rise from the shadows and whisper the same question:
"Why did God allow it?"
Few verses in all of Scripture answer that question with more power, more depth, and more hope than Genesis 50:20.
After decades of suffering, slavery, false accusations, imprisonment, loneliness, and unimaginable heartbreak, Joseph stood face to face with the very brothers who had destroyed his life.
They expected revenge.
Instead, they received one of the most breathtaking declarations in the entire Bible.
In Hebrew, Genesis 50:20 reads:
"וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה"
Ve'atem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
A faithful translation is:
"You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good."
Not merely, "God used it."
Not merely, "God fixed it."
Not merely, "God worked around it."
The Hebrew verb chashav carries the idea of planning, weaving, devising, or designing.
Joseph is saying something astonishing.
The brothers planned.
God planned.
The brothers had intentions.
God had intentions.
Their intentions were evil.
God's intentions were good.
The same event carried two completely different purposes.
This verse does not teach that evil becomes good.
It teaches that God remains sovereign even while evil men freely choose evil.
That distinction matters.
God never becomes the author of sin.
The brothers remain guilty.
Their jealousy was real.
Their hatred was real.
Their cruelty was real.
Yet their wickedness never escaped the boundaries of God's sovereign rule.
What looked like chaos on earth was never chaos in heaven.
That truth changes everything.
Because most of us spend years trying to understand the pit.
Joseph spent years in one.
Before becoming second only to Pharaoh, he was abandoned by family.
His own brothers stripped him of his robe.
They threw him into a cistern.
They sold him like property.
Imagine the horror.
The people who should have protected him became the very people who profited from his pain.
Many readers know the story so well that they forget how traumatic it really was.
Joseph wasn't merely inconvenienced.
He was betrayed.
The deepest wounds are rarely caused by strangers.
They come from people whose names we know.
People we trusted.
People we loved.
People we expected to stay.
Perhaps that is why Joseph's story continues to grip hearts thousands of years later.
Because many people reading this know exactly what betrayal feels like.
You know what it feels like to cry alone.
You know what it feels like to wonder whether God sees.
You know what it feels like to ask why your life turned in a direction you never chose.
Joseph knew that feeling too.
Then came Potiphar's house.
For a moment, things seemed better.
Scripture says the LORD was with Joseph.
Yet even there, suffering followed.
Potiphar's wife falsely accused him.
His integrity became the reason for his imprisonment.
Think about that.
Sometimes doing what is right does not immediately improve your circumstances.
Sometimes obedience costs you.
Joseph honored God and ended up in prison.
That reality shatters the prosperity gospel.
Faithfulness does not guarantee comfort.
Faithfulness guarantees God's presence.
There is a difference.
Years passed.
Not days.
Not weeks.
Years.
The dreams God gave Joseph seemed impossible.
The promises appeared forgotten.
The silence must have been deafening.
Yet heaven had not forgotten.
God was writing a story Joseph could not yet read.
That is one of the deepest meanings of Genesis 50:20.
God's providence is often invisible until the final chapters.
We judge God by individual pages.
God sees the entire book.
The New Testament echoes this truth repeatedly.
Paul writes in Romans 8:28:
Kai oidamen hoti tois agapōsin ton Theon panta synergei eis agathon.
"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good."
Paul does not say all things are good.
He says God works all things together for good.
Even the painful things.
Even the confusing things.
Even the things that still make you cry years later.
The cross itself proves this.
No event in history was more evil than the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
Humanity murdered the only sinless man who ever lived.
Yet Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's predetermined plan and foreknowledge.
The greatest evil ever committed became the means of the greatest salvation ever offered.
That is Genesis 50:20 on a cosmic scale.
What Joseph experienced points directly to Jesus.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers.
Jesus was rejected by His own people.
Joseph was sold for silver.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Joseph suffered unjustly.
Jesus suffered perfectly.
Joseph saved many lives through his suffering.
Jesus saves eternally through His suffering.
The shadow points to the substance.
The servant points to the Savior.
The story points to Christ.
And this is where Genesis 50:20 becomes intensely personal.
Many people want God to explain their pain.
God often offers something greater.
His presence within it.
There are wounds you still do not understand.
There are prayers that seemed unanswered.
There are chapters that still feel unfinished.
Yet Joseph teaches us that God's silence is not God's absence.
His delay is not His neglect.
His hiddenness is not abandonment.
The God who was working in the prison was the same God working in the palace.
The God who was working in betrayal was the same God working in promotion.
The God who was working in suffering was the same God working in salvation.
Nothing was wasted.
Nothing.
Not the tears.
Not the waiting.
Not the loneliness.
Not the injustice.
Not the years.
Not even the pit.
Because God wastes nothing surrendered to Him.
Perhaps that is why Genesis 50:20 continues to comfort believers generation after generation.
It gives us permission to acknowledge evil honestly while trusting God's goodness completely.
Joseph did not minimize what happened.
Notice carefully.
He did not say:
"You meant well."
He did not say:
"It wasn't that bad."
He did not say:
"Let's pretend it never happened."
He called evil exactly what it was.
Evil.
Biblical forgiveness never requires denying reality.
Truth comes before healing.
Yet Joseph also saw a greater reality.
God's hand was bigger than man's sin.
That is the miracle.
Not that evil disappeared.
But that evil never won.
And perhaps someone reading this desperately needs that reminder today.
The betrayal did not win.
The divorce did not win.
The addiction did not win.
The diagnosis did not win.
The abuse did not win.
The grief did not win.
The grave did not win.
Jesus Christ won.
The resurrection is the ultimate declaration that evil never gets the final word.
God does.
And His final word is grace.
That is the heartbeat of our mission.
Because that is exactly what Joseph's life demonstrates.
A scandalous betrayal became a story of redemption.
A pit became a pathway.
A prison became preparation.
A tragedy became testimony.
What looked like destruction became deliverance.
What looked like the end became the beginning.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is what He is doing in your life right now.
Maybe the chapter that feels broken is not the final chapter.
Maybe the pain that feels pointless is still being woven into a purpose you cannot yet see.
Maybe heaven is writing a greater story than the one your eyes can currently read.
And maybe years from now, standing on the other side of what today feels impossible, you will finally understand why God never let go.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
You may never know whose faith is hanging by a thread and needs this reminder today.
What pit did God bring you out of?
Your testimony may become someone else's lifeline.
Supporting this ministry is one practical way of helping spread the Gospel, disciple believers, and point people to Jesus Christ around the world.

Because every share spreads truth.
Every comment creates community.
Every testimony glorifies Christ.
One day you may discover that the chapter you begged God to remove became the chapter He used most powerfully to reveal Himself.
